passage:
Thursday night
Dinner with Madhav at the Irani café. He ordered, then asked the same thing twice. In the middle of the story about his sister's engagement he stopped and said, "Sorry, I just remembered the vendor invoice." Then the tax form. Then his bike service. His chai went cold. He said he's been sleeping badly, waking at three and thinking about "stuff". I asked him to write all the stuff on a napkin. Eleven things! Half were ten-minute jobs. We put a day next to each one, and he took a photo of the napkin. He looked lighter when we left, though maybe I'm imagining it. I'll ask him on Monday how he slept.
Darshan

qa.q: How many things did Madhav list on the napkin?
qa.a: Eleven things.

qa.q: What does Madhav waking at three thinking about "stuff" suggest about his mind?
qa.a: His many half-done jobs seem to circle in his head at night, draining his sleep as well as his attention at dinner.

qa.q: Why was putting a day next to each item a useful step?
qa.a: It turned a vague cloud of jobs into a plan, so Madhav's mind no longer had to hold every open task at once, and half of them turned out to be ten-minute jobs.

qa.q: What was dinner like for Darshan before the napkin list?
qa.a: Darshan kept losing Madhav mid-conversation, even during the engagement story, which may have felt like eating with someone only half there.

passage: The dhaba by the Nabha bus stand was loud with trucks, but Baljeet noticed Lokesh wasn't hearing any of it. He stirred his dal without eating, checked his phone, put it face down, checked it again. "The loan files, the cooperative meeting, my brother's college form, the roof before the rains," he muttered when Baljeet asked. "I lie awake going through them." Baljeet pulled out a pay-slip envelope and slid it across with a pen. "Write them all. Then a day next to each." Lokesh wrote nine lines. Two he crossed out as "not mine to do." The roof got Sunday. When the rotis came, he finally tore one, ate, and asked Baljeet about the new calf at home.

qa.a: At the dhaba by the Nabha bus stand.

qa.a: He seemed anxious and pulled in many directions by unfinished jobs, from the loan files to the roof, and couldn't settle into the meal.

qa.q: What did writing the list let Lokesh decide?
qa.a: He saw that two items weren't his to do and crossed them out, and gave the roof a day, so the pile shrank and each remaining job had a place.

qa.q: How might the evening have gone for Baljeet if nothing had been said?
qa.a: Baljeet would likely have eaten beside a friend who kept stirring cold dal, and Lokesh would have gone home to lie awake with the same list in his head.

passage: At the injera place near Bole Road in Addis Ababa, Abebe watched his colleague Yara tear her bread into smaller and smaller pieces without eating any. He'd asked about her sister's wedding twice. Both times she said, 'Sorry, what?' Then she picked up her phone, put it down, picked it up. 'The grant report,' she said finally. 'And the landlord's email. And I promised the intern feedback. And my visa papers.' She rubbed her eyes. 'I wake at four going through them.' Abebe took a pen from his pocket and turned a paper napkin over. 'Say them all. I'll write.' There were nine. Next to each, she gave a day: Tuesday, Thursday, 'not this month'. When the list was done, Yara folded it into her wallet. Then she ate, properly, and asked about his mother for the first time all evening.

qa.q: How many things were on Yara's list?
qa.a: There were nine.

qa.q: What does Yara tearing her bread without eating suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests her mind was stuck on unfinished tasks, and she was too anxious and distracted to enjoy the meal or the conversation.

qa.q: What did Abebe suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: He wrote every task on a napkin and had her give each one a day, so the open loops had a place and stopped pulling at her attention.

qa.q: How might the rest of the dinner have felt for Abebe after the list?
qa.a: Abebe probably felt relieved and more connected, since Yara finally ate and asked about his mother for the first time all evening.

passage: At two in the morning, the hospital staff canteen in Kochi was nearly empty. Elizabeth carried two plates of upma to the corner table and sat across from Anjali, who was on her third night shift in a row. Anjali stirred her food and stared at the wall. 'You with me?' Elizabeth asked. 'Hm? Sorry.' She had asked the same question twice. 'It's the discharge summaries,' Anjali said. 'Four still open. And the audit form. And I told Amma I'd call about the gas cylinder. I lie down after shift and they all start talking.' Elizabeth pulled a spare duty roster from her pocket and turned it over. 'Tell me each one. We'll give it a time.' Summaries before handover. Audit on Friday. Amma at lunch. Anjali read the list twice, then took her first real bite. 'Oh. I'm starving.'

qa.q: Where were Elizabeth and Anjali eating?
qa.a: They were in the hospital staff canteen in Kochi at two in the morning.

qa.q: How can you tell Anjali's mind was on unfinished tasks?
qa.a: She stirred her food, stared at the wall, asked the same question twice, and said the tasks all start talking when she lies down.

qa.q: What small step did Elizabeth offer, and what did it change?
qa.a: She wrote each task on the back of a duty roster with a time for it, and Anjali could finally relax enough to eat.

qa.q: How might Anjali's next rest after shift be different?
qa.a: With each task given a time on paper, the tasks may stop talking in her head, so she might finally sleep.

Subject: last night's dinner
Hi Divyansh,
Thanks for coming to the farewell last night. I hope you don't mind me writing this.
All evening you looked somewhere else. You checked your phone during the toast. When Meenal asked about your trip, you said "sorry, what?" twice. At one point you said, half to yourself, "I still haven't sent the vendor sheet." Then the audit mail. Then your visa form.
I know that feeling. Last year I had eleven half-done things in my head and didn't sleep properly for weeks.
What helped me: one list, every open task, and next to each one, a day and time. Once they were scheduled, my head let go of them.
Want to try it together on Saturday over coffee?
Siddharth

So, this is Mahima, and you asked what I noticed about burnout at work. I'll tell you about a dinner with Tejas.
We'd gone out for his birthday, six of us, a nice rooftop place. And Tejas was there, but not there. Every few minutes he'd pull out his phone, type something, put it back. He laughed a second late at jokes. When the cake came, he said, "Wait, did I reply to the client about the invoice?"
Later I asked him how he was sleeping. He said badly, lying awake going through a list that never ended. So on the way home I said, "Write every half-done thing down tonight. Then give each one a slot in your calendar. Your brain's holding all of it open." He texted the next day, "Did it. Slept seven hours."

qa.q: What did Tejas ask about when the cake came?
qa.a: He asked, "Wait, did I reply to the client about the invoice?"

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling as Tejas kept pulling out the phone?
qa.a: Mahima felt worried and a bit sad, noticing that Tejas was physically at the birthday but mentally elsewhere.

qa.q: Why did Mahima's suggestion help Tejas sleep?
qa.a: Writing down every half-done thing and giving each a calendar slot closed the open loops, so his mind stopped circling them at night.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt at his own birthday dinner?
qa.a: Tejas probably felt scattered and tired, unable to enjoy the evening because so many tasks were left open.

passage:
I'm Rehana. Rafiq and I have shared a desk for two years, so I notice when he's off.
Last Friday a few of us went for biryani after work. Rafiq ordered, then forgot what he'd ordered. He kept opening his notes app, scrolling, closing it. When someone asked about his sister's wedding, he said, "Sorry, I was thinking about the deck. And the tax form. And the leaking tap."
I can't say what was going on inside his head. But he looked tired in a way sleep hadn't fixed.
On the walk to the metro I said, "Do you want to dump everything onto one page? Then just give each thing a day." We did it on a bench under a streetlight. Fourteen items. He put a date next to each.
He said it felt like putting down a heavy bag.

qa.q: How many items did Rafiq list on the bench?
qa.a: There were fourteen items.

qa.q: What might Rehana have been feeling at the biryani dinner?
qa.a: Rehana likely felt concerned, noticing Rafiq was tired in a way sleep hadn't fixed and kept drifting to half-done tasks.

qa.q: What small step helped Rafiq, and why?
qa.a: Putting everything on one page and giving each item a day helped, because scheduled tasks stop quietly pulling at attention.

qa.q: How does Rafiq describe the change after listing the tasks?
qa.a: Rafiq said it felt like putting down a heavy bag, suggesting real relief.

Tenzin, you've read that same email four times. Let me, Kishore, tell you about my friend Bala. We were twenty-five, sharing a room in Chennai, both working at the same bank. One Sunday we went for biryani and he didn't taste a single bite. His eyes kept sliding to the window. "The branch audit, the loan files, my sister's college form, the scooter papers," he said. "All half-done." He was sleeping badly for weeks.
So one night I tore a page from my ledger and said, "Write them all. Now put a day next to each." He grumbled, but he did it. The next Sunday he ate two plates.
So, before you read that email a fifth time: how many open things are sitting in your head?

qa.a: They went for biryani.

qa.q: What was young Kishore feeling as Bala stared at the window?
qa.a: Kishore felt worried for Bala, noticing the friend was eating without tasting and sleeping badly.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Bala?
qa.a: Writing all his half-done tasks on the ledger page and putting a day next to each.

qa.q: What were those weeks like for Bala?
qa.a: He was tired and distracted, unable to enjoy food or sleep because unfinished tasks kept pulling at him.

At dinner in a Kolkata restaurant, Reena noticed Kamal wasn't really there. He stirred his soup and checked his phone. When she told him about her trip, he said, "Hmm? Sorry."
"What's going on?"
"Nothing. Just... the client report, the leaking tap, my sister's visa form, the bank thing. None of it's done."

He wrote six things. Then, next to each, a day: Tuesday, Wednesday, Saturday.
He put the napkin in his wallet. Ten minutes later, he was laughing at her story about the airport.

passage:
Last month my friend Simran came over for dinner. I'm Indu. She'd been looking tired for weeks.
At dinner she kept stopping mid-sentence. "Sorry. I just remembered I haven't sent the invoice. And the plumber. And the insurance form." She said she hadn't slept well in days.
I got a notebook from my shelf. "List them. All of them."
She wrote eleven things. Some were tiny. Then I asked her to write a day next to each. Three she crossed out entirely.
She looked at the page and let out a long breath. "I feel like I put down a heavy bag."
The next week she told me she was sleeping better.

qa.q: How many things did Simran write?
qa.a: She wrote eleven things.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling watching Simran stop mid-sentence?
qa.a: Indu felt concerned, noticing how tired and distracted Simran had been for weeks.

qa.q: Why did the list help Simran?
qa.a: Writing down and scheduling the unfinished tasks closed the loops, so they stopped draining her attention and sleep.

qa.q: How does Simran feel after writing the list?
qa.a: She feels relieved and lighter, like she put down a heavy bag.
